title: The Case Against Dirty Empowerment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The target here is a specific hypocrisy the author names dirty empowerment: announcing delegation while retaining control. The essay first sets out genuine empowerment — the leader sets strategy, delegates critical tasks, holds people accountable to outcomes rather than methods, and serves as a resource during execution — and notes the well-documented performance advantage of empowered teams over directed ones. Control-hungry leaders, unable to resist, second-guess decisions, wade into detail and take over day-to-day execution, which communicates distrust more loudly than the original announcement communicated confidence. The sharpest claim is comparative: this half-measure is more demotivating than honest micromanagement would have been, because the gap between stated and actual autonomy breeds grievance and the corrosive we-versus-them dynamic. The piece attributes the pattern to organisational fashion — empowerment is so universally promoted that leaders pay lip service without intending to give anything up — and ends by reframing the requirement not as courage but as ambition to succeed through others.
points: The coinage ‘dirty empowerment’ names a half-delegation that the author argues is worse than open control, because the announced autonomy makes the subsequent interference read as distrust.
The behavioural signature is listed concretely: second-guessing decisions, getting into the details, and diving into day-to-day execution after having delegated.
The author traces the pattern to institutional fashion — empowerment is so strongly promoted that leaders adopt the vocabulary without the intention.
The predicted organisational cost is a we-versus-them mentality that the piece treats as specifically destructive to high performance.
The closing reframe denies that empowerment requires courage, calling it instead an ambition to succeed through others.
quotes: They hold others accountable to outcomes and give away as much influence over the process and everyday decisions as the team can handle.
Leaders who empower others set strategy and then delegate critical tasks to others, giving them the autonomy to decide how to achieve agreed-upon outcomes.
By second-guessing decisions, getting involved in the details, and diving into the day-to-day execution, they show the team they are not to be trusted.
This so-called dirty empowerment is even more demotivating than if the leader simply maintained tight control to begin with.
Because most contemporary organizations strongly promote the idea of empowerment, many leaders feel compelled to pay it lip service without any intention of actually giving up control.
They grouse and complain, often creating the “we-versus-them” mentality that is so destructive to high performance.
Spending time on strategy, key metrics, and resource allocation moves the team forward much faster than controlling the minutiae of execution.
